title: Words with Two Meanings
theme: Multiple meanings in nature and play
objectives: I can tell that one word can have two meanings.
I can use the sentence around a word to choose its meaning.
I can draw and say a sentence for each meaning of a word.
I can tell a partner which meaning a word has in a story.
rationale: Second graders know bark, bank, and bat as everyday words, but many do not yet notice that the same spelling can name two different things. This unit teaches eight nature and play words with two familiar meanings. Each word's main meaning comes first, and a second meaning is taught on purpose, so children practice the key reading habit of using the rest of the sentence to choose between them. Unit 12 returns to the idea with school and play words.

passage.title: Creek Day
paras: In spring, Mia and her dog walked to the creek. She sat on the muddy bank and tossed a rock into the water. A bat began to fly over the trees. Her dog gave a loud bark.
A little wave rolled past the rock. Mia felt the rough bark of the old tree, too.

qs.q: What does "bark" mean in this sentence: Her dog gave a loud bark?
qs.why: A dog makes the sound, so bark means a dog's loud sound here.
The story says she sat on the muddy bank of the creek.

qs.q: What season is it in the story?
qs.why: The first sentence says In spring.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight common nature and play words that each have two meanings. The main meaning is taught first and the second one on purpose, so children practice choosing a meaning from the clues in a sentence. Draw two quick pictures for each word to make both meanings clear. Unit 12 revisits the idea with school and play words.

notes.va.bark.n: Teach the tree meaning first and the dog sound second. Show both pictures. Children often know only the dog sound, so use a real photo of tree bark if possible. Spanish speakers: corteza for tree bark, ladrido for the sound.
notes.va.bank.n: The river meaning is the main sense here. Children usually know bank for money, so connect the two by showing a river picture beside a money picture. Ask which clue word helps.
notes.va.wave.n: The water meaning comes first. The hand meaning is the second sense. Do both actions: use a hand wave and a pretend ocean wave. Clue words: water, beach, hello.
notes.va.spring.n: Children may know spring only as the season. Show the coil as a real object (a pen spring or toy). The two meanings share only the word, so avoid searching for a link.
notes.va.bat.n: Have children say whether they picture a flying animal or a baseball bat, then check the clue words in the sentence. Bats are mammals; they are not blind and are not birds.
notes.va.rock.n: Rock is a stone first and a back-and-forth movement second. Do not teach the music meaning in this unit. Use a real rock and a rocking chair or a baby doll.
notes.va.fly.v: Fly is a verb first (to move in the air) and the insect second. The past form is flew. Some children say flied; model flew gently in context.
notes.va.seal.n: Seal is a sea animal first and a verb meaning to close second. Show a seal photo and an envelope. Seals are mammals that breathe air, not fish.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The sentence says a bat flew out of the cave at dusk. A cave and flying are clue words. A baseball bat cannot fly by itself, so this bat is the animal. The clue words tell me the meaning.'
discuss: What clue words in a sentence help you choose a meaning for bark?
Which of these words can you act out two ways?
misconceptions: Children may think the two meanings of a word must be related. They are different words that happen to share a spelling.
Some children think each word has only one correct meaning. Show two meanings together in a quick picture pair.
Children may confuse bark (tree) with the dog sound; emphasize clue words like tree and dog.
extend: Make a class chart with a picture and a sentence for each meaning.
Find a two-meaning word in a read-aloud and decide which meaning the author used.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit whisper, curious, and eager with this unit's words: a curious child might whisper near a bat cave, and an eager child might fly a kite. Add them to a class talk routine.
